I don't know how many customer support folks we have, but it's not very many, 30, 40, I'm not sure, way smaller than you would have at any comparable company, and it's because we've automated a lot of our flows. We've got most questions using our internal resources, knowledge base, guidelines for how we answer questions, what kind of personality, et cetera. You can teach the model those things and then have it do a lot of its answers automatically, or where it doesn't have the full confidence to answer a particular question, it can still suggest an answer, request a human to look at it and then that human's answer actually is its own sort of fine tuning data for the model. You're telling it the right answer in a particular case. (01:02:29): We're using... At various places. Some of these places, you want a little bit more reasoning, is not super latency sensitive, so you want a little more reasoning, and we'll use one of our O series models. In other places, you want a quick check on something and so you're fine to use four oh mini, which is super fast and super cheap. In general, it's like specific models for specific purposes and then you ensemble them together to solve problems. By the way, again, not unlike how we as humans solve problems, a company is arguably an ensemble of models that have all been fine tuned based on what we studied in college and what we have learned over the course of our careers. We've all been fine tuned to have different sets of skills and you group them together in different configurations and the output of the ensemble is much better than the output of any one individual.
turns.zh: 接下来是我们内部技术栈的部分。我举个例子。客户支持部门每周有超过4亿活跃用户，我们收到了大量用户咨询。尽管我不确定具体有多少客服人员，但确实不多，大概30到40人，这远比其他同类公司少得多。这是因为我们对许多业务流程进行了自动化处理。大多数常见问题都能通过内部资源、知识库、回答指南和个性化设定来解决。模型可以学习这些规则，从而自动生成答案。若模型对某个问题信心不足时，会给出建议性回答，并请人工核查。人工核查后的结果反过来又会成为模型微调的数据，帮助模型不断优化。（01:02:29）我们在不同场景下使用不同模型。有些场景对延迟要求不高，可以使用O系列模型；而有些场景需要快速校验时，则选用速度极快且成本低廉的四Oh Mini模型。总之，针对不同需求选用特定模型，再将它们组合起来，就能解决问题。这与人类解决问题的方式颇为相似——一家公司本质上就是由基于大学所学和职业生涯积累的知识进行微调的模型集合，每个人都具备不同技能组合，通过不同配置组合起来，最终产出远超单个个体的智慧成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kevin, you're blowing my mind. That sounds exactly correct. And also, different people, you pay them less, they cost less to talk to, some people take a long time to answer, some people hallucinating. This is...
turns.zh: 凯文，你真是让我惊叹不已。这听起来太准确了。还有，不同的人薪资不同，沟通效率也不同，有些人回复慢，有些人甚至会胡言乱语。这真是……

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: I'm telling you. This is a mental model but really does work in thinking...
turns.zh: 我跟你说。这种思维模型确实很管用……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, right. Yeah. This is great. Some people are visual, they want to dry out their thinking, some people want to talk word cell. Wow, this is a really good metaphor. So again, coming back to your advice here because I love that we circled back to it, you're finding a really good way to think about how to design great AI experiences and LMs, I guess, specifically is think about how a person would do this.
turns.zh: 哦，对。太棒了。有些人善于视觉化，他们想理清思路；有些人则喜欢用文字表达。哇，这真是个绝妙的比喻。所以回到你之前的建议——我特别喜欢你又回到了这个点上——你找到了一个思考如何设计出色的AI体验和语言模型的绝佳方法，我猜具体来说就是设身处地从人的角度去思考。

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Well, it's maybe not always the answer is to think about how a person would do it, but sometimes to gain intuition for how you might solve a problem, you think about what an equivalent human would do in those situations and use that to at least gain a different perspective on the problem.
turns.zh: 嗯，也许不总是要从人的角度出发，但有时为了获得解决问题的直觉，你可以想想在类似情况下人类会怎么做，然后利用这个思路至少获得一个不同的视角。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, this is great.
turns.zh: 哇，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Because some of this really is talking to a model. There's a lot of prior art because we talk to other humans all the time and encounter them in all sorts of different situations, and so there's a lot to learn from that.
turns.zh: 因为有些情况确实是在和模型对话。毕竟我们日常和人类交流时也会遇到各种情况，所以这里有很多可以借鉴的经验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so speaking of humans, I want to chat about the future a little bit. So you have three kids, and a community member asked me this hilarious question that I think it's something a lot of people are thinking about. So this is Patrick [inaudible 01:04:47]. I worked with him at Airbnb. He says ask what he's encouraging his kids to learn to prepare for the future. I'm worried my 6-year-old by the year 2036 will face a lot of competition trying to get into the top roofing or plumbing programs and need a backup plan.
turns.zh: 好的，说到人类，我想聊聊未来。你们有三个孩子，有位社区成员问了我一个特别有趣的问题，我觉得这也是很多人都在思考的。这位叫帕特里克的朋友（01:04:47），我在Airbnb时和他共事过。他问我，如何让孩子们学会为未来做准备。我担心我6岁的孩子到2036年面对激烈的竞争，争取进入顶尖的屋顶修缮或管道安装项目时，会需要一个后备计划。

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: That's funny. So our kids, we have a 10 year old and eight year old twins, so they're still pretty young. It's amazing how AI native they are. It's completely normal to them that there are self-driving cars. That they can talk to AI all day long. They have full conversations with Chat GPT and Alexa and everything else. I don't know, who knows what the future holds? I think things like coding skills are going to be relevant for a long time, who knows? But I think if you teach your kids to be curious, to be independent, to be self-confident, you teach them how to think, I don't know what the future holds, but I think that those are going to be skills that are going to be important in any configuration of the future. And so it's not like we have all the answers, but that's how Elizabeth and I think about our kids.
turns.zh: 这真有趣。我们家有10岁和8岁的双胞胎孩子，所以他们还很小。令人惊讶的是，他们对人工智能的熟悉程度堪称天生。自动驾驶汽车对他们来说再正常不过，他们整天和人工智能对话。和Chat GPT、Alexa等平台的对话对他们来说轻而易举。我不知道未来会怎样，但我认为编程技能在很长一段时间内都会很重要，谁知道呢？不过我觉得如果教会孩子们保持好奇心、独立自主、自信自立，教会他们如何思考问题，我觉得无论未来如何变化，这些技能都会很重要。我们并非无所不知，但伊丽莎白和我就是这样看待孩子的教育的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And do you find that AI... There's a lot of talk about AI tutoring. Is that something you guys are doing? I know they're using Chat GPT, I love all the photos you post where they're playing with prompts and stuff, but I guess is there anything there you're experimenting with or you think is going to become really important?
turns.zh: 你们觉得人工智能...现在有很多关于人工智能辅导的讨论。你们有在做这方面的尝试吗？我知道你们在用Chat GPT，我很喜欢你们发的那些孩子们玩Prompt的照片，但我想你们是否也在尝试其他可能变得非常重要的技术？

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: This is something that... It's maybe the most important thing that AI could do. Maybe that's a grand statement. There are lots of important things that AI can do, including speeding up the pace of fundamental science research and discovery, which maybe is actually the most important thing AI can do. But one of the most important things would be personalized tutoring. And it kind of blows my mind that there is still... I know there are a bunch of good products out there. Khan Academy does great things. They're a wonderful partner of ours. Vinod Khosla has a non-profit that's doing some really interesting stuff in this space and is making an impact. But I'm kind of surprised that there isn't a 2 billion kid AI personalized tutoring thing because the models are good enough to do it now, and every study out there that's ever been done seems to show that when you have... Like, education is still important, but when you combine that with personalized tutoring, you get multiple standard deviation improvements in learning speed. (01:07:31): And so it's uncontroversial, it's good for kids, it's free. Chat GPT is free, you don't need to pay, and the models are good enough. It still just kind of blows my mind that there isn't something amazing out there that our kids are using and your future kids are using, and people in all sorts of places around the world that aren't as lucky as our kids to be able to have this sort of built-in, solid education. Again, Chat GPT is free. People have Android devices everywhere. I really just think this could change the world and I'm surprised it doesn't exist and I want it to exist.
turns.zh: 这可能是人工智能能做的最重要的事情之一。也许这话说得太夸张了。人工智能能做很多重要的事情，包括加速基础科学研究和发现的步伐，这或许才是人工智能最重要的贡献。但最重要的应用之一肯定是个性化辅导。让我震惊的是，现在居然还没有一个价值20亿美元的儿童人工智能个性化辅导项目。模型现在已经足够成熟，可以做到这一点了。所有已有的研究似乎都表明，当把教育和个性化辅导结合起来时，学习速度能提升多个标准差。（01:07:31）这毫无争议，对孩子们有益，而且免费。Chat GPT是免费的，无需付费，模型也足够成熟。仍然让我难以置信，为什么没有一个令人惊叹的产品，让我们的孩子、未来的孩子以及世界各地不像我们这么幸运、无法获得这种系统化优质教育的人都能使用。再说一次，Chat GPT是免费的。到处都有安卓设备。我真的觉得这能改变世界，我很惊讶它还不存在，我希望它能出现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This kind of touches on something I want to spend a little time on, which is a lot of people also worry a lot about AI, where it's going, they worry about jobs it's going to take, they worry about the super intelligence squashing humanity in the future. What's your perspective on that and just the optimistic case that I think people need to hear?
turns.zh: 这让我想多谈谈一个话题，即许多人对人工智能的发展深感担忧。他们担忧它将取代大量就业岗位，担忧超级智能未来会压制人类。关于这些问题，您有何看法？尤其是，我认为人们需要听到的乐观观点是什么？

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: I mean, I'm a big technology optimist. I think if you look over the last 200 years, maybe more, technology has driven a lot of the advancements that have made us the world and the society that we are today. It drives economic advancements, it drives geopolitical advancements, quality of life, longevity advancement. I mean, technology's at the root of just about everything, so I think there are very few examples where this is anything but a great thing over the longer term. That doesn't mean that there aren't...
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我是个技术乐观主义者。回顾过去200年甚至更久的历史，技术推动了诸多进步，成就了我们今天的世界和社会。它促进了经济发展、地缘政治进步、生活质量提升、寿命延长。可以说，技术几乎渗透到方方面面。因此，我认为从长远来看，人工智能绝非坏事。这并不意味着不存在……

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: ... a great thing over the longer term. That doesn't mean that there aren't temporary dislocations or where there aren't individuals that are impacted, and that matters too. So it can't just be that the average is good. You've got to also think about how you take care of each individual person as best you can. (01:09:18): It is something that we think a lot about and as we work with the administration, as we work with policy, we try and help wherever we can. We do a lot with education. One of the benefits here is that ChatGPT is also perhaps the best reskilling app you could possibly want. It knows a lot of things. It can teach you a lot of things if you're interested in learning new things. (01:09:43): These are very real issues. I'm super optimistic about the long run, and we're going to need to do everything we can as a society to ensure that we make this transition as graceful and as well-supported as we can.
turns.zh: 就长期而言，这确实是一件好事。但这并不意味着不会出现暂时的混乱，也不意味着不会有个人受到影响，而这些问题同样值得关注。因此，仅关注平均数据是不够的。我们还必须尽最大努力关怀每一位个体。（01:09:18）这是我们深思熟虑的问题。在与政府合作、制定政策时，我们会尽可能提供帮助。我们在教育领域投入了大量精力。ChatGPT或许是目前最出色的再培训应用程序之一，它知晓诸多知识。如果你有学习新技能的意愿，它能为你提供丰富的指导。（01:09:43）这些都是实实在在的问题。我对长远前景持乐观态度，但作为一个社会，我们需要竭尽全力确保这一转型尽可能平稳且获得充分支持。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To give people a sense of where things might be going. That's a big question in a lot of people's minds. So someone asked this question that I love, which is, "AI is already changing, creative work in a lot of different ways, writing and design and coding, what do you think is the next big leap? What should we be thinking is the next big leap in AI-assisted creativity specifically, and then just broadly, where do you think things are going to be going in the next few years?"
turns.zh: 为了让人们对未来趋势有所把握。这是许多人心中的重大疑问。有人曾向我提出一个我很喜欢的疑问：“人工智能已经以多种方式改变着创意工作，比如写作、设计和编程。您认为下一个重大突破是什么？具体而言，在人工智能辅助的创意领域，我们应当关注哪些方向？更宏观地看，在未来几年里，您认为整个行业将朝着哪个方向发展？”

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Yeah. This is also an area where I'm a big optimist. If you look at Sora, for example. I mean we talked about ImageGen earlier and the absolute fount of creativity that people are putting across Twitter and Instagram and other places. I am the world's worst artist like the worst. Maybe the only thing I'm worse at than art is singing. Give me a pencil and a pad of paper and I can't draw better than our eight-year-old. But give me ImageGen and I can think some creative thoughts and put something into the model and suddenly have output that I couldn't have possibly done myself. That's pretty cool. (01:11:09): Even you look at folks that are really talented. I was talking to a director recently about Sora, someone who's directed films that we would all know, and he was saying, for a film that he's doing, take the example of some sort of sci-fi-ish, think of Star Wars, and you've got some scene where there's a plane zooming into some Death Star-like thing. And so you've got the plane looking at the whole planet, and then you want to cut to a scene where the plane's kind of at the ground level, and all of a sudden you see the city and everything else. How are we going to manage that cut scene? And that transition? (01:11:51): And he was saying, "In the world of two years ago, I would have paid a 3D effects company a hundred grand and they would've taken a month, and they would've produced two versions of this cut scene for me. And I would've evaluated them. We would've chosen one, because what are you going to do? Pay another 50 grand and wait another month. And we would've just gone with it. And it would be fine. Movies are great. I love them. And there've been..." (01:12:25): Obviously, we can do great things with the technology that we've had, but you now look at what you can do with Sora. And his point was, "Now, I can use Sora, our video model, and I can get 50 different variations of this cut scene just me brainstorming into a prompt and the model brainstorming a little bit with me. I've got 50 different versions. And then of course, I can iterate off of those and refine them and take different ideas. And now I'm still going to go to that 3D effects studio to produce the final one, but I'm going to go having brainstormed and had a much more creative approach with an outcome that's much better. And I did that assisted by AI." (01:13:08): My personal view on creativity in general is that it's no one's going to... You don't type into Sora like, "Make me a great movie." It requires creativity and ingenuity, and all these things, but it can help you explore more. It can help you get to a better final result. So, again, I tend to be an optimist in most things, but actually, I think there's a very good story here.
turns.zh: 是啊。这也是我非常乐观的一个领域。比如说索拉（Sora）吧。我之前提过ImageGen，还有人们在推特、Instagram等平台上展现出的无穷创意。我自己算世界上最差劲的艺术家了，可能除了画画之外，我最不擅长的就是唱歌了。给我一支铅笔和一张纸，我画出来的东西连八岁小孩都比不上。但用ImageGen，我就能构思出一些创意想法，输入到模型里，然后突然就能产出超出我个人能力的成果。这真是太棒了。（01:11:09）：就连那些才华横溢的人也不例外。我最近和一位导演聊起索拉，他执导过我们都熟知的电影。他说，在他正在制作的一部科幻片里，有个场景是飞机飞向类似死星的物体。飞机先是俯瞰整个星球，然后镜头切换到地面视角，突然就能看到城市和其他景象。怎么实现这个切换呢？（01:11:51）：他说：“两年前，要是让我找3D特效公司做这个，得花十万美元，耗时一个月，还只能做出两个版本让我评估。最后选一个版本，接着再等一个月再花五万美元来完善。这样做电影太糟糕了。我热爱电影，也见证了……” （01:12:25）：显然，现有技术也能做出不错的东西，但看看索拉能带来什么。他的观点是：“现在我用索拉的视频模型，自己构思提示词，再让模型辅助思考，就能得到50个不同版本的切换场景。然后我还能在此基础上进行迭代和优化，最终再找3D特效公司完成最终制作，但这次我已经有了更成熟的创意和思路。”（01:13:08）：我对创意的总体看法是，没有人能……你不会对索拉说：“给我拍一部大片吧。” 这需要创造力和巧思，但它能帮助你探索更多可能，获得更好的最终成果。所以，总的来说，我对大多数事物都持乐观态度，但我确实认为这里有很好的机遇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know Sam Altman, I think it was him who tweeted recently, the creative writing piece that you guys are working on where it's... He is very bad at writing creative stuff, and he shared an example where it's actually really good. I imagine that's another area of investment.
turns.zh: 我认识山姆·奥特曼，我记得是他最近在推特上分享的创意写作例子。他自己写东西很糟糕，但分享的例子却很棒。我想这也是值得投资的领域之一。

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Yeah, there's some exciting stuff happening internally with some new research techniques. We'll have more to say about that at some point. But yeah, Sam sometimes likes to show off some of the stuff that's coming, which is smart. By the way, it's very indicative of this iterative deployment philosophy. We don't have some breakthrough and keep it to ourselves forever, and then bestow it upon the world someday. We kind of just talk about the things we're working on and share when we can and launch early and often, and then iterate in public. I really like that philosophy.
turns.zh: 是的，公司内部正在进行一些令人兴奋的研究技术开发。我们稍后会详细介绍。但没错，山姆有时喜欢展示即将推出的新成果，这很明智。顺便说一句，这恰恰体现了我们迭代式部署的理念。我们不会把突破性成果藏着掖着，最后再一次性公布，而是尽可能多地分享进展，早早发布并频繁迭代，最后在公开场合进行优化。我真的很欣赏这种理念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love all these hints that a few things coming. I know you can't say too much. You talked about how there might be a coding leap coming in the near future maybe by the time this comes out. Is there anything else people should be thinking about, might be coming in the near future? Any things you can tease that are interesting? Exciting?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你透露的这些即将推出的新功能的暗示。我知道你不能多说。但你提到可能在不久的将来会有编码方面的突破，也许就在这期播客发布的时候。接下来还有什么值得期待的新进展吗？有没有其他即将问世的有趣技术？令人兴奋的消息？

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Man, this hasn't been enough for you?
turns.zh: 天啊，你还嫌不够？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Only everything is getting better every day.
turns.zh: 一切都在日新月异地进步。

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Yeah. I'm like, man, I hope we get some of this stuff out before the episode launches so-
turns.zh: 是啊。我就想，天哪，希望我们能在这一期播客发布前把这些成果推出来——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is your new timebox.
turns.zh: 这就是你的新时间节点。

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: ... I don't piss people off. The amazing thing to me is we were talking earlier about how far models have come in just a couple of years. If you went back to GPT-3, you'd be disgusted by how bad it was, even though Lenny of two years ago was mind-blown by how good these were. And for a long time, we were iterating every six to nine months on a new GPT model. It was like GPT-3, GPT-3.5, 4, and now with this o-series of reasoning models, we're moving even faster. Every roughly three months, maybe four months, there's a new o-series model, and each of them is a step up in capability. (01:15:41): And so the capabilities of these models are increasing at a massive pace. They're also getting cheaper as they scale. You look at where we were even a couple of years ago. I think the original, I don't know, what was it, GPT-3.5 or something was like 100 x the cost of GPT-4o mini today in the API. A couple of years, you've gone down two orders of magnitude in cost for much more intelligence. And so I don't know where there's another series of trends like that in the world. Models are getting smarter, they're getting faster, they're getting cheaper, and they're getting safer too. They hallucinate less every iteration. (01:16:27): And so the Morse Law and transistors becoming ubiquitous. That was a law around doubling the number of transistors on a chip every 18 months. If you're talking about something where you're getting 10 x every year, that's a massively steeper exponential. And it tells us that the future is going to be very different than today. The thing I try and remind myself is, the AI models that you're using today is the worst AI model you will ever use for the rest of your life. And when you actually get that in your head, it's kind of wild.
turns.zh: ……我可不想惹人生气。对我来说，最惊人的是我们之前讨论的，模型在短短几年内取得的巨大进步。如果回看GPT-3，你会对它糟糕的表现感到震惊，而两年前的莱尼却对其卓越的表现惊叹不已。长期以来，我们每六到九个月就会迭代一个新的GPT模型。先是GPT-3、GPT-3.5、GPT-4，现在又有了o-系列推理模型，我们的进展速度更快了。大约每三个月，甚至四个月，就会推出一个新的o-系列模型，每个模型都比前一个有更大的能力提升。（01:15:41）：因此这些模型的能力正在以惊人的速度提升。随着规模扩大，成本也在降低。看看几年前的我们。我记得最初的GPT-3.5之类的模型，API上的成本是今天GPT-4o mini的100倍。短短几年间，成本下降了两个数量级，却换来了更强的智能。真不知道世界上还有哪种技术能有这样的指数级增长。模型越来越智能、速度越来越快、成本越来越低，安全性也越来越高，每次迭代产生的幻觉越来越少。（01:16:27）：就像摩尔定律和晶体管的普及。那个定律是每18个月晶体管数量翻倍。但如果你谈论的是每年增长10倍的技术，那就是指数级增长得多了。这告诉我们，未来将与今天大不相同。我努力提醒自己，你今天使用的AI模型，将是余生中使用的最差的AI模型。当你真正意识到这一点时，真是令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to actually say the same thing, and that's the thing that always sticks with me when I watch this thing. You're talking about Sora, and I imagine many people hearing that are like, "No, no. It's not actually ready. It's not good enough. It's not going to be as good as a movie I see in the theater." But the point is what you just made that this is the worst it's going to be. It will only get better.
turns.zh: 我其实也想说同样的话，这也是我每次看这段内容时最深有感触的地方。你谈到Sora，我相信很多听众都会说：“不，不。它还没准备好。它还不够好，不可能比得上我在影院看的电影。” 但关键在于你刚刚提到的，这已经是最糟糕的阶段了。之后只会越来越好。

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Yeah, model maximalism. Just keep building for the capabilities that are almost there, and the model's going to catch up and be amazing.
turns.zh: 是啊，模型至上主义。只要不断提升那些几乎触手可及的能力，最终模型就会迎头赶上并创造惊喜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Escape to where the puck is going to be.
turns.zh: 追随冰球的轨迹，顺势而为。

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me, I was just using... I was duplifying everything the other day and I was just like, "What is taking so long."
turns.zh: 这让我想起前几天我在复制所有内容时，还一直在想：“怎么要花这么久时间？”

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: As one does.
turns.zh: 就像人们常说的那样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just like cut... What was that?
turns.zh: 就像剪辑……那是什么？

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: I said, as one does.
turns.zh: 我说，就像人们常说的那样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As one does these days. I was just like, "It's taking a minute to generate this image of my family in this amazing way." Come on, what's taking so long. You just get so used to magic happening in front of you.
turns.zh: 就像如今人们常说的那样。我当时就想：“用这种惊艳的方式生成家庭照片怎么要花一分钟时间？”得了吧，这有什么好慢的？你只是太习惯于眼前魔术般的效果了。

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Yeah, totally.
turns.zh: 是啊，一点没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, final question. This is going to go in a completely different direction. A lot of people asked about this. So famously, you led this project at Facebook called Libra, which is now called Novi. A lot of people always wondered, "What happened there? That was a really cool idea." I know some people have a sense there's regulation challenges, things like that. I don't know if you've talked about this much. So I guess, could you just give people a brief summary of just what is Libra? This project you working on, and just what happened, and how you feel about it?
turns.zh: 好，最后一个问题。这个问题会转向一个完全不同的方向。很多人都问过这个问题。众所周知，你在Facebook领导了一个叫Libra的项目，现在改名为Novi了。很多人一直好奇：“那到底发生了什么？那可是个很酷的想法。” 我知道有些人觉得里面有监管挑战之类的问题。我不知道你是否谈过太多。所以我想，你能不能给人们简单概括一下Libra到底是什么？你参与的这个项目，到底发生了什么，以及你对此的看法？

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, David Marcus led it, and I happily work for him and with him. I think he's a visionary and also a mentor and a friend. Honestly, Libra is probably the biggest disappointment of my career. When I think about the problems we were solving, which are very real problems. If you look at, for example, the remittance space, people sending money to family members in other countries, it is maybe... I mean it's incredibly regressive, right? People that don't have the money to spend are having to pay 20% to send money home to their family. So outrageous fees, it takes multiple days, you have to go then pick up cash from... It's all bad. (01:19:11): And here we are with 3 billion people using WhatsApp all over the world, talking to each other every day, especially friends and family, and exactly the kind of people who'd send money to each other. Why can't you send money as immediately, as cheaply, as simply as you send a text message? It is one of those things when you sit back and think about it, that should just exist. And that was what we set out to try and do. (01:19:41): Now, I don't think we played all of our cards perfectly. If I could go back and do things, there are a bunch of things I would do differently. (01:19:50): We tried to get it all at once. We tried to launch a new blockchain. It was a basket of currencies originally. It was integration into WhatsApp and Messenger, and I think the whole world kind of went like, "Oh my God, that's a lot of change at once." And it happened also to be at the time that Facebook was at the absolute nadir of its reputation. And so that didn't help. It was also not the Messenger that people wanted for this kind of change. We knew all that going in, but we went for it. (01:20:21): I think there are a bunch of ways that we could do that that would've introduced the change a little bit more gently, maybe still gotten to that same outcome, but fewer new things at once and introduced the new things one at a time. Who knows? Those were decisions we made together. So we all own them. Certainly, I own them. But it fundamentally disappoints me that this doesn't exist in the world today because the world would be a better place if we'd been able to ship that product. I would be able to send you 50 cents in WhatsApp for free. It would settle instantly. Everybody would have a balance in their WhatsApp account. We'd be transact... I mean, it should exist. (01:21:03): I don't know. To be honest, the current administration is super friendly to crypto. Facebook's reputation, Meta's reputation is in a very different place. Maybe they should go build it now.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，大卫·马库斯领导了这个项目，我很乐意为他工作，也很享受与他共事的时光。我认为他是个有远见的人，同时也是导师和朋友。说实话，Libra项目可能是我职业生涯中最大的遗憾。当我回想起我们当时要解决的问题——那些实实在在存在的难题时。比如汇款领域，人们给身处其他国家的家人汇款，这简直……我是指这太不人道了，对吧？那些没有余钱的人却要花20%的手续费才能把钱寄回家。手续费高得离谱，转账还需要数天时间，还得亲自去领现金……简直糟透了。（01:19:11）如今全球有30亿人每天通过WhatsApp相互交流，尤其是亲友之间，这正是他们最常相互转账的场景。为什么不能像发短信一样即时、低廉、简单地转账呢？当你静下心来思考这个问题时，它本该自然而然地存在。这正是我们当初努力要实现的目标。（01:19:41）现在回想起来，我们确实没有把每件事都处理得完美。如果能重来，我会做出很多不同选择。（01:19:50）我们试图一口气解决所有问题。我们试图推出全新区块链，最初是货币篮子，然后整合到WhatsApp和Messenger平台。但当时整个世界仿佛在说："天哪，一下子变动太多了！"而Facebook当时正处于声誉最低谷，这无疑雪上加霜。此外，Messenger也不是人们期望用于此类变革的平台。我们事前就清楚这些问题，但还是选择全力推进。（01:20:21）我认为有很多改进方案能更平稳地引入变革，或许最终结果相同，但一次只推出一个新功能，逐步推进。谁知道呢？这些都是我们共同做出的决定。所以责任由我们所有人共同承担。当然，我也深感遗憾，因为如果我们当时能成功推出这款产品，世界会变得更美好。比如我在WhatsApp上免费给你转50美分，就能即时到账。每个人都能在WhatsApp账户里存钱。我们本可以实现交易……这本该存在的。（01:21:03）说实话，当前政府对加密货币非常友好，Facebook和Meta的声誉也已大为改观。或许他们现在应该去开发它了。

turns.en: I was looking at the history of it, and apparently, they sold the tech to some private equity company for 200 million bucks.

turns.en: Yeah, yeah, and-
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，还有——

turns.en: They had to buy it back.

Aptos and Mistin are two companies that are built off of this tech. So at least all of the work that we did, did not die and lives on in these two companies, and they're both doing really well. But still, we should be able to send each other money in WhatsApp, and we can't today.
turns.zh: 现在有几家区块链公司基于这项技术开发产品，因为技术从一开始就是开源的。Aptos和Mistin就是两家基于此技术的公司。所以至少我们所做的一切努力并没有白费，仍体现在这两家公司中，而且它们发展得都很不错。但即便如此，我们现在还是无法在WhatsApp上给彼此转账。

turns.en: Let's do it. Okay. What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 开始吧。好的。你有没有两三本你最常向别人推荐的书？

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Co-Intelligence by Ethan Mollick, a really good book about AI and how to use it in your daily life as a student, as a teacher. He's super thoughtful. Also, by the way, a very good follow on Twitter. The Accidental Superpower by Peter Zion. Very good if you're interested in geopolitics and the forces that sort of shape the dynamics happening. And then I really enjoyed Cable Cowboy, I don't know who the author is, but the biography of John Malone. Just fascinating. If you like business, especially if you want to get into... I mean the man was an incredible dealmaker and shaped a lot of the modern cable industry. So that was a good biography.
turns.zh: 伊桑·莫利克的《协同智能》。这本书讲AI，以及如何在日常生活中运用它，无论是作为学生还是教师。他思路非常深刻。顺便说一句，他在Twitter上也很值得关注。彼得·齐奥恩的《无意的超级大国》。如果你对地缘政治和塑造现代动态的力量感兴趣，这本书很棒。还有我非常喜欢的《有线电视牛仔》，我不知道作者是谁，但这是约翰·马龙的传记。太精彩了。如果你对商业感兴趣，尤其是想涉足……要知道他是个了不起的交易高手，对现代有线电视行业影响深远。所以这是一本很棒的传记。

turns.en: These are all first-time mentions, which is always a great,
turns.zh: 这些都是首次提及的，总是很棒。

turns.en: Oh, good.

turns.en: But I like the idea. I want more Americana. I want more being proud of being strong. And I thought Top Gun 2 did a really good job of that. Pride and patriotism, I think the US could use more of that.
turns.zh: 但我喜欢这个主意。希望能多一些美国风情，多一些为强大而自豪的感觉。我觉得《壮志凌云2》在这方面做得很棒。自豪和爱国主义，我觉得美国可以多一些。

turns.en: Yeah. So actually, this is interestingly enough, it is more of a philosophy, but then I thought Zuck encapsulated it one time on a Facebook earnings call. So I actually had this made into a poster. It sits in my room. But somebody was asking Mark. This is literally on an earnings call, so it's like an analyst on an earnings call asking him. It was some quarter when Facebook had grown a lot. This was back in the 20 teens sometime, I think. But he's like, "So what did you do? What was it that you launched? What was the one thing that drove all this growth for you?" And he said something to the effect of, "Sometimes it's not any one thing, it's just good work consistently over a long period of time." And that's always stuck with me. (01:25:33): And I think it is. I mean I run ultra marathons. It's like it's just about grinding. I think people too often look for the silver bullet when a lot of life and a lot of excellence is actually showing up day in and day out, doing good work, getting a little bit better every single day, and you may not notice it over a week or even a month. And a lot of people then kind of get dismayed and stop. But actually, you keep doing it. The gains keep compounding. And over the course of a year, two years, five years, it adds up like crazy. So good work consistently over a long period of time.
turns.zh: 有的。说起来挺有意思的，这更像是一种哲学理念，但我记得扎克伯格在一次Facebook财报电话会议上概括过。所以我把这句话印成了海报，挂在自己房间里。但之前有人问马克·扎克伯格这个问题。这句话就是在财报电话会议上说的，当时有分析师问他："Facebook增长这么快，你们做了什么？推出了什么产品？是什么因素推动了这一切增长？"扎克伯格回答大意是：“有时候没有什么神奇的秘诀，只是长期持续地做好工作。" 这句话一直让我印象深刻。（01:25:33）：我觉得确实如此。比如我跑超级马拉松，关键就是坚持不懈。我觉得很多人总想寻找速成之道，而生活中的许多成就和卓越实际上是日复一日地做好工作，日积月累，虽然一周或一个月看不出效果，但长期坚持就能看到成果。所以长期持续地做好工作真的很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I got to make a poster of this now. That is-
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这句话了。我现在就得去把它做成海报。这真是——

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: We'll get you one.
turns.zh: 我们会给你准备一份。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I so resonate with that. Okay, I'll take it. That is so good. Okay, final question. I'm going to ask if you have any prompting tricks, and I'm going to set it up first. But think about if you have a trick that you could recommend to people for prompting LLMs better. I had a guest, Alex Komorowski, come on the podcast. He's from Stripe and writes his weekly reflections on what's happening in the world. A lot of them are AI-related. (01:26:36): And he once described an LLM as a zip file of all human knowledge. All the answers are in there, and you just need to figure out the right question to ask to get the answer to every problem basically. And so it just reminded me how important prompt engineering is and knowing how to prompt well. You're constantly prompting ChatGPT. What's one tip, one trick that you found to be helpful in helping you get what you want?
turns.zh: 我太认同这句话了。好的，我接受这个观点。这太棒了。最后一个问题。我想问你有没有什么提示技巧，我先抛个题目。但你有没有什么建议，能帮助人们更好地提示LLM（大语言模型）？我邀请过嘉宾亚历克斯·科莫罗夫斯基上节目。他来自Stripe，每周都会写反思文章，内容多与AI相关。（01:26:36）：他曾把LLM描述成人类所有知识的压缩包。所有答案都在里面，你只需要找到正确的问题，就能得到每个问题的答案。这让我意识到提示工程的重要性，以及如何有效地进行提示。你一直在提示ChatGPT。你有什么有用的技巧或窍门吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Well, I'll say, first of all, I want to kill the idea that you have to be a good prompt engineer. I think if we do our jobs, that stops being true. It's just one of those sharp edges of models that experts can learn. But then, just over time, you shouldn't need to know all that. The same way you used to have to get deep into, "What's your storage engine in MySQL? Are you using InnoDB 4.1?" There's still use cases for that if you're at the deep edge of MySQL performance. But most people don't need to care. And you shouldn't need to care about minute details of prompting if AI is really going to become broadly adopted. (01:27:39): But today, we're not totally there. I think by the way, we are making progress there. I think there is less prompt engineering than there had to be before. But in line with some of the fine-tuning stuff I was talking about and the importance of giving examples, you can do effectively poor man's fine-tuning by including examples in your prompt of the kinds of things that you might want and a good answer. So like, "Here's an example and here's a good answer. Here's an example, and here's a good answer. Now, go solve this problem for me." And the model really will listen and learn from that. (01:28:15): Not as well as if you do a full fine-tune, but much more than if you don't provide any examples. And I think people don't do that often enough.
turns.zh: 好吧，我首先要说，我想打破一个观念，那就是你必须成为一个出色的提示工程师。我认为只要我们做好本职工作，这种观念就站不住脚了。这只是模型中的一些难点，而专家们可以掌握这些知识。但随着时间推移，你其实不需要了解所有这些细节。就像过去你必须深入探究“MySQL的存储引擎是什么？你用的是InnoDB 4.1吗？”之类的问题一样——如果你深入研究MySQL性能优化，这种方法仍有用。但对大多数人来说没必要深究。同样，如果AI要真正普及，你也不需要过度关注提示的细微差别。（01:27:39）但目前我们还做不到这一点。我得说我们在这方面确实在进步。现在需要的提示工程师比以前少多了。但结合我之前提到的微调技巧以及提供示例的重要性，你可以通过在提示中加入示例来实现类似的低成本微调，比如“这里有个示例和正确答案。现在去解决这个问题吧。”模型真的会听从指令并从中学习。（01:28:15）虽然效果不如全面微调，但比不提供示例要好得多。我觉得人们用得还不够多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. One tip that I heard, I'm curious if this works is you tell it, "This is very, very important to my career." Make it really understand like, "Someone will die if you don't answer me correctly." Does that work?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我听说过一个技巧，不知道有没有用，就是你对它说：“这对我的职业生涯非常非常重要。”让它真正理解，比如“如果你不能正确回答，我的人生就完了”。这样行得通吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: It's really weird. There's probably a good explanation for this. But you can also say things. So, yes, I think there is some validity to that. You can also say things like, "I want you to be Einstein. Now, answer this physics problem for me," or, "You are the world's greatest marketer, the world's greatest brand marketer. Now here's a naming question." And there is something where it sort of shifts the model into a certain mindset that can actually be really positive.
turns.zh: 确实挺奇怪的。这背后可能有合理的解释。但你也可以试试。比如，“我希望你成为爱因斯坦。现在给我解答这个物理问题吧”，或者“你是最伟大的营销人员，全球最顶尖的品牌营销专家。现在这里有个命名问题。”这样能让模型进入特定思维模式，效果确实不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I use that tip all the time actually. I always... When I'm coming up with questions for interviews and I use it occasionally to come up with things I haven't thought of, I actually type, "You're the world's best podcast interviewer."
turns.zh: 我经常用这个技巧。每次为面试出题时，我偶尔会用它来激发灵感，比如输入“你是最出色的播客采访者”。

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have Kevin Weil coming on the pod... Yeah, it actually works.
turns.zh: 我邀请了凯文·韦尔来参加播客……确实有效。

turns.speaker: Kevin Weil
turns.en: By the way, back to our other point that we made a few times. You do do that sometimes with people. You sort of put them... You frame things, you get them into a certain mindset, and the answer is completely different. So I think there are human analogs of this one more time.
turns.zh: 顺便说回我们之前多次提到的观点。有时候你也会对人这样做。你会给他们设定框架，让他们进入特定思维模式，答案就会完全不同。所以我觉得这其中有可以类比人类思维的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kevin, this was incredible. I was just thinking about a way to end this. The way I feel like... I feel like not only are you at the cutting edge of the future.
